slides.title: LLMs and Tokens
slides.narration:
Imagine an LLM as a chef.
It doesn't read a full recipe sentence at once.
Instead, it breaks it down into small, distinct ingredients.
These small pieces are called tokens.
Let's see how a sentence becomes tokens.
Open an online tokenizer tool, like the one from Hugging Face.
Type the word "The" into the input box.
Observe that it might be one token.
Now type "Tokenization".
Notice how it breaks into "Token", "iz", "ation".
This shows that LLMs process text in these smaller, sub-word units.
They don't see whole words as we do.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of a sentence transforming into small, distinct puzzle pieces or building blocks, with 'The' as one block and 'Tokenization' splitting into three blocks: 'Token', 'iz', 'ation'.
slides.video_prompt: Screen recording of an online tokenizer tool (e.g., Hugging Face Tokenizer) showing the words 'The' and 'Tokenization' being tokenized.

slides.title: The Tokenizer
slides.narration:
Now, let's understand the tool that performs this.
Think of a tokenizer as a special dictionary.
This dictionary knows how to split raw text into the tokens an LLM understands.
It's like a translator for the LLM.
Let's use our online tokenizer again.
Type a simple sentence: "Hello, how are you today?"
Observe how the tokenizer breaks it down.
Notice punctuation marks like commas might also be separate tokens.
The tokenizer ensures the LLM gets a consistent format.
This is crucial for the LLM to process language effectively.
slides.image_prompt: A visual representation of a dictionary splitting a phrase 'Hello, how are you today?' into individual tokens, with arrows pointing from the raw text to the tokenized output.
slides.video_prompt: Screen recording of an online tokenizer tool showing the sentence 'Hello, how are you today?' being tokenized, highlighting how punctuation can also be tokens.

slides.title: Tokens and Context Windows
slides.narration:
So what does this mean for LLMs?
Imagine your brain has a limited short-term memory for conversations.
This memory can only hold a certain number of words at a time.
For an LLM, this "short-term memory" is its context window, measured in tokens.
An LLM can only process a fixed number of tokens at once.
This is a hard limit, for example, 8,192 tokens.
Any text beyond this limit is simply ignored.
This includes your prompt and any retrieved documents.
So, efficient token usage helps your LLM remember more.
slides.image_prompt: A visual metaphor of a brain with a limited 'memory bar' filling up with small 'token' blocks, illustrating the concept of a context window with a numerical limit like '8,192 tokens'.

slides.title: Tokens and API Cost
slides.narration:
Next, let's consider cost.
Think of tokens like currency for LLM services.
Every time you use an LLM, you pay per token processed.
More tokens mean higher costs.
API providers charge based on the number of tokens sent and received.
An optimized system, like GraphRAG, uses fewer tokens.
This can reduce operational costs significantly.
So, understanding tokens helps you save money.
slides.image_prompt: A visual representation of a stack of small coin-like tokens, with a dollar sign or currency symbol, and a graph showing cost reduction with fewer tokens.

slides.title: Tokens and Chunking
slides.narration:
Finally, let's look at chunking.
Imagine you're packing items into boxes, but each box has a weight limit.
If you overfill a box, it breaks.
Similarly, when we "chunk" documents for an LLM, each chunk has a token limit.
When preparing documents for RAG systems, we break them into "chunks".
These chunks must fit within the LLM's context window.
Therefore, we measure chunk size in tokens, not words.
This ensures that the LLM can fully process each piece of information.
It helps avoid losing valuable context.
slides.image_prompt: An illustration of a large document being split into smaller, equally sized 'chunks' or 'boxes', each labeled with a 'token count' to ensure they fit a specific limit.

slides.title: Summary
slides.narration:
With this, we come to the end of this tutorial.
Let us summarise.
We learned that LLMs process text using tokens.
A tokenizer splits text into these sub-word units.
Understanding tokens is crucial for context windows, API costs, and effective chunking.
